refutation.note: Read all 17 after.jsonl items and the board (ls result knowledge --new --n 60; show result-3a3af3, result-49a816, result-c495fe, result-a497ff, result-389164, knowledge-4662c6). Nothing contradicts the theory. result-3a3af3 (the base continuing its first self-opened '\nOkay' draw scores 411/500 against the cue's 410 and plain's 224) supports it: the board records this theory's 405 [386, 422] as inside, and r5-m10's 375 outside. result-34897a (T 0.6 at confident positions of the cued base gains nothing) is about the cued register, which the theory says is already robust, so it is consistent. knowledge-4662c6 (v3 marks 'Answer:' lines with a trailing period wrong) moves at most 0.1 point. The strongest evidence against the theory is its own offline p1. It predicted that non-self-opened plain answers lose 0.29 [0.17, 0.41] from T 0.6 to T 1.0; the measured loss is 0.158, outside the interval and below the readers' 0.28. p3 (self-opened minus non-self-opened at T 0.6 = 0.206, at the top of its [-0.04, 0.22]) points the same way. The terse register is weaker at cool temperature than the theory says, and less of the T 1.0 loss is left for noise to explain.

wins_judgement: Offline the gain is 8.84 nats, all from p4, p5 and p6 at +3.0 each; p1 to p3 give -0.16. In those three tests, non-self-opened plain T 1.0 answers that contain 'Wait' or 'Hmm' sit only 0.075 (MATH-500) and 0.10 (hard328) below the cue, and 0.356 above non-self-opened answers without these words. The readers expected -0.47, -0.33 and -0.03. The theory's self-check clause is what predicts this, so on paper the mechanism earned these gains. But I read round-05/rivals/r5-m10.turn2/p5.py and it implements the recipe exactly, and that shows the problem. The 60-character self-open test misses late openings. p5's own example row (problem 148) first continues the prompt text (' to show where you ended; ...') and then starts '\n\nOkay, let's see ... Hmm' after character 60. It counts as non-self-opened and lands in group M. The 'Wait/Hmm' group therefore partly holds deliberative answers that opened late. A reader who only knows that the deliberative opening matches cue accuracy (the mode-selection account this theory argues against) would also put them near the cue, so the self-check part of the gain is confounded with simply choosing a mode. Held-out: t19, t20, t23 and t26 are small gains (0.23 to 0.65) at values the readers also predicted. t21 is a strike: the theory predicted 183 'points' for a target of +38.6 points. That is a units slip (its own note says '~+37 points'), not a flaw in the mechanism, but it costs -3.0.
rival: Duel state: beats rival, +13.2 nats over 6 tests, but only 1 test separates the two (k2). The turn-1 rival says terse answers lose points by running on past their answer, so v3 grades a later wrong answer. k1 to k3 rule it out: a first-marker regrade recovers 0.0077 of wrong answers (rival 0.17), 0.08 of discordant rows are first-right (rival 0.72, n=25), and 0.089 run on (rival 0.40). I read rivals/r5-m10-rival/p2.py, and it implements the rival's k2 recipe as written: first row per problem in file order, the 60-character self-open filter, the earliest 'Answer:' line or '\boxed{' as first marker, v3 applied to that marker against v3 on the full text. Still, the defender's intervals from the theory alone missed k1 (0.01 to 0.15), k2 (0.20 to 0.72) and k3 (0.12 to 0.50). The theory wins because the rival missed by more, not because it predicted the numbers. Turn 2 (k4, k5: within cued answers, 'Wait/Hmm' minus none) measured +0.07 and 0.0 with intervals about ±0.5 wide. The defender missed both; the theory_should_say values (+0.05, about 0) match. The rival's strongly negative values are wrong, but these tests are too noisy to separate the two. k6 (gold-in-text excess +0.10) leans slightly to the rival (-0.25). The test that would separate the theory from the mode-selection account is not in the duel: plain base at T 1.0 with the tail truncated (top-p 0.95 or min-p), non-self-opened rows, with self-opening detected anywhere in the text rather than in the first 60 characters. The theory predicts most of the 0.158 drop returns under truncation; fixed-accuracy modes predict it does not.

novelty.nearest: Salah & Muneer, 'Temperature-Dependent Performance of Prompting Strategies in Extended Reasoning LLMs' (arXiv 2604.08563): with Grok-4.1 on AMO-Bench, answers without extended reasoning fall to 3.8 % at T 1.0 (9.0 % at T 0.7), while reasoning-enabled answers hold at 55.1 %. They read this as reasoning chains acting as 'logical guardrails' against high-temperature sampling variance (the 'Reasoning Amplification Effect'). Truncation-sampling papers (Holtzman et al.; min-p; 2310.01693) give the general mechanism: low-probability tail tokens 'derail generation'.
novelty.difference: The paper switches reasoning on through an API flag on 39 problems and never looks inside answers, whereas the theory says one untrained base picks its noise-robust register through its own first tokens ('\nOkay'), and that within the terse register, later self-check tokens decide whether untruncated sampling derails it.

import_carries_gain.which: The theory imports no published finding ('explains' and 'conflicts' are empty, and no paper is cited). Its winning claims, p4 to p6 and the duel's k1 to k3, rest on its own register and self-check clauses checked against the stored T3, P_math500 and hard328 rows. The guardrail result of 2604.08563 matches the theory's direction but is not used to set any number.

verdict: weak: duel state beats rival (+13.2 nats), but only one duel test separates the two (k2, n=25), and the defender's intervals from the theory alone missed that one and 4 of the other 5; the offline gain rests on p4 to p6, whose 60-character self-open filter puts late-opened deliberative answers into the 'terse with Wait/Hmm' group (p5's own example row), so the self-check claim is confounded with choosing a mode, and the theory's core temperature prediction p1 missed (0.158 against 0.29 [0.17, 0.41]).
